extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders in drinking-water rulemaking (EPA scientists, public health researchers, state regulators, public water systems, and public commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and technical guidance for EPA's development, justification, and scientific support of a National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) and MCLG for perchlorate, including statutory tests, modeling approach, study selection, and systematic review standards. Intended to inform rulemaking, public comment, and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility standard for treatment technologies (small/medium systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feasible means technically possible and affordable; EPA historically has not set different standards based solely on what is reasonably afforded by small and medium systems. If the EPA cannot identify any affordable technologies for a particular category of small systems, the EPA must identify variance technologies that 'achieve the maximum reduction or inactivation efficiency that is affordable' and protect public health (SDWA section 1412(b)(15)(A) and (b)(15)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations about what treatment is 'feasible' must consider both technical possibility and affordability. Where no affordable full-scale technology exists for small systems, identify alternative/variance technologies that maximize reduction consistent with affordability and protection of public health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice timing and reporting for MCL violations (SDWA §1414(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a final NPDWR is in effect and an MCL has been established, public water systems (PWSs) must provide notice to the public if the water system fails to comply with an applicable MCL; the Administrator 'shall by regulation . . . prescribe the manner, frequency, form, and content for giving notice.' For violations that could have serious adverse effects from short-term exposure, notice must 'be distributed as soon as practicable, but not later than 24 hours' after the PWS learns of the violation, and the system must report the violation to both the State and the Administrator within that same time period (SDWA §1414(c)(2)(C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public notice rules should specify format, timing, frequency, and content. For potential short-term serious health effects, prioritize immediate distribution (within 24 hours) and simultaneous reporting to State and EPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping, monitoring, reporting, and information provision (SDWA §1445(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person subject to SDWA requirements 'shall establish and maintain records, make reports, conduct monitoring, and provide information to the Administrator as reasonably required by regulation' to assist the Administrator in establishing regulations, determining compliance, administering assistance programs, evaluating health risks, and advising the public (SDWA §1445(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemakings should specify the records, monitoring frequency, reporting forms, and information provision obligations necessary for regulatory and public-health functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: RfD derivation methodology (example: NRC/EPA perchlorate RfD)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPC used a reference dose (RfD) of 0.7 μg/kg/day for perchlorate in 2005 based on a no-observed-effect level (NOEL) of 7 μg/kg/day (from inhibition of radioactive iodine uptake, a 'non-adverse' precursor) and application of a total uncertainty factor (UF) of 10 to account for intraspecies variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RfD derivation should identify the relevant critical effect or precursor, select an appropriate point of departure (e.g., NOEL), and apply documented uncertainty/safety factors (with justification) to account for inter- and intra-species variability and data limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory criteria for a regulatory determination (SDWA §1412(b)(1)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether to regulate a contaminant, EPA must evaluate: (1) whether the contaminant may have an adverse effect on the health of persons; (2) whether the contaminant is known to occur or there is a substantial likelihood that it will occur in public water systems with a frequency and at levels of public health concern; and (3) whether, in the Administrator's sole judgment, regulation presents a meaningful opportunity for health risk reduction for persons served by PWSs (the three statutory criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A positive regulatory determination requires satisfaction of all three statutory prongs; analyses should present evidence and reasoning for each prong (health effects, occurrence/frequency/levels, and meaningful opportunity for risk reduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of life-stage susceptibilities and PBPK model use
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models that predict iodide uptake inhibition (RAIU) across sub-populations and life stages. EPA adjusted models and sought peer review to ensure appropriateness for assessing health outcomes, and also evaluated whether to apply the NRC RfD directly to sensitive life stages as an alternative to model-based HRLs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing health risk, explicitly consider sensitive life stages (pregnant women, fetuses, infants), evaluate suitability and uncertainties of PBPK models for those life stages, and document model adjustments and peer-review outcomes. Consider alternatives (e.g., life-stage-specific application of an RfD) and transparently justify choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mode-of-action and PBPK/PD-IUI modeling; extend BBDR (SAB recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: SAB recommended deriving an MCLG using a mode-of-action approach and physiologically-based pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic iodide uptake inhibition (PBPK/PD-IUI) modeling and extending a Biologically Based Dose-Response (BBDR) model to link early events with subsequent events (iodide deficiency, thyroid hormone changes) and their relationship to neurodevelopmental outcomes during sensitive early life stages. SAB recommended focusing on maternal hypothyroxinemia (decreases in fT4) as a key indicator rather than hypothyroidism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt modeling frameworks that integrate MOA and PBPK/PD to address life-stage susceptibilities and connect precursor events to downstream adverse outcomes (e.g., neurodevelopment). Select endpoints most appropriate for predicting adverse outcomes (e.g., maternal fT4/hypothyroxinemia) and justify endpoint selection relative to the MOA and available data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step BBDR modeling approach for perchlorate
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA developed a two-step BBDR modeling approach: (1) estimate serum fT4 levels in iodine-deficient pregnant women in the first trimester following perchlorate exposure; (2) relate maternal fT4 levels to neurodevelopmental health effects in offspring using epidemiological data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling frameworks used to derive MCLGs should specify the mechanistic steps, quantify intermediate biomarkers (e.g., fT4), and integrate epidemiological dose–response information to estimate adverse outcomes. Document model inputs, assumptions, and validation/peer-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemiological study selection criteria for dose–response modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated 71 epidemiological studies and selected five for dose–response assessment; Korevaar et al. (2016) was chosen to inform BBDR modeling because it had sufficient quantitative data for modeling (3,600 usable mother/child data pairs), appropriately addressed confounding variables, and assessed an adverse neurodevelopmental endpoint (decreased IQ in children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select studies for quantitative modeling based on objective criteria: sample size and usable data pairs, ability to address confounding, relevance of endpoints to adverse outcomes, and sufficiency of quantitative information for dose–response modeling. Document study-selection rationale and peer-review of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Reproducible
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic review requires thorough documentation at all steps to enable reproducibility of assessment conclusions by the scientific community and the public. The 2025 draft TSD followed EPA systematic review methods and documented methods/results (e.g., sections 4–6 and appendices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reproducibility by documenting search strategies, inclusion/exclusion criteria, study-evaluation methods, data extraction, and analysis so independent reviewers can reproduce conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency requires extensive documentation of every step (e.g., literature search terms, study relevancy screening criteria, study evaluation results) and public accessibility of those materials (e.g., via HAWC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, public documentation of search terms, screening criteria, evaluation results, and decision-making so stakeholders can review the evidence base and assessment choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Communicative of error and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic review processes should clearly document and communicate potential errors and uncertainties (e.g., in reference dose derivation, epidemiological evidence base, and sensitivity for specific populations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize and discuss uncertainty sources, quantify where possible, and communicate implications for risk conclusions and regulatory decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Collaborative and interdisciplinary
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic review development requires technical experts from multiple fields (epidemiology, toxicology, statistical modeling, public health) to ensure comprehensive evaluation and strengthen scientific rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble interdisciplinary teams and document contributor roles and expertise to show that multiple scientific perspectives informed assessment decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Skeptical of findings and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate potential bias of individual studies, follow an evidence determination framework, and document uncertainties; the process supports skepticism of findings and assumptions through rigorous study-evaluation steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply pre-defined bias-evaluation frameworks, perform independent evaluations by multiple scientists, and explicitly document how study limitations affect confidence and evidence integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Structured for falsifiability of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use criteria agnostic to results to identify relevant studies, evaluate studies for potential bias, perform evidence determination and integration, and document uncertainty; these steps permit falsifiability by relying on pre-defined, result-agnostic criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-specified protocols and result-agnostic inclusion criteria so hypotheses can be falsified or supported based on systematic evidence collection and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Subject to unbiased peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify studies from peer-reviewed literature databases agnostic of results and subject foundational science and models to independent external peer review (e.g., SAB and two independent panels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on peer-reviewed sources and subject models/assessments to external, transparent peer review processes; document peer-review comments and resulting changes or rationale for not adopting recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Accepting of negative results as positive outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature identification and evidence-integration process is agnostic to study results; negative or null findings are included in study evaluation and can lead to evidence determinations such as 'evidence inadequate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include and account for null/negative studies in evidence integration; explicitly consider how inconsistent or negative results affect overall confidence and regulatory conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic review principle — Without conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps are taken to minimize conflicts of interest (COI) by using peer-reviewed literature with COI statements and, when necessary, requiring additional independent peer review to meet Information Quality guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document COI vetting steps, prefer peer-reviewed sources with COI disclosures, and perform additional COI-focused reviews where journal COI reporting is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-available-science requirement and updating between determination and proposal (SDWA §1412(b)(3)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must ensure the MCLG is based on the best available science and must account for changes in science after it makes its determination to regulate but before it proposes the NPDWR; new data and analyses can alter whether prior determinations remain supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before proposing a rule, reassess and incorporate new peer-reviewed science and occurrence data to ensure the MCLG and regulatory determinations reflect the best available information; document any changes and their impact on statutory criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence and exposure analysis for 'meaningful opportunity' determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess occurrence (e.g., from UCMR data), estimate percentage of water systems and populations with detections above health reference levels, and use these occurrence estimates to evaluate whether regulation would present a meaningful opportunity for health risk reduction. Small percentages of systems exceeding HRLs may support a conclusion of no meaningful opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representative occurrence data, clearly state assumptions and population estimates (including sensitive subpopulations), and tie occurrence estimates quantitatively to the statutory 'meaningful opportunity' prong of the regulatory determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model adjustment transparency and peer review requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When EPA adjusts models (e.g., PBPK) prior to using them for regulatory decision-making, the Agency should have those adjustments peer-reviewed to ensure the model is appropriate for assessing health outcomes and to make modeling uncertainties transparent to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document any model adjustments, make them available for external review, solicit peer-review feedback on uncertainty and applicability, and incorporate reviewer recommendations or explain why not adopted.
